title: Down the Ore Line
passages:
The back room was warm, which was the first wrong thing. The second was the man on Teodoro's couch, breathing.

Wren stopped inside the door. Rhea's knife had left her wrists bare and pale where the tape had been, and she rubbed one against the other without knowing she did it.

"Three," she said.

Marlowe looked at her. Gray around the mouth, one shoulder strapped down under a cargo-strap splint, the other arm laid across his stomach like something he was keeping from rolling off. He didn't say anything.

"Two."

That was the wall. She'd carried those two numbers since Bay 4, since the lid came down and Voss's stamp came down on the seal and her own voice went counting in her ears. She'd come four hundred kilometers and walked into a warm room to say the rest of it to the man in the box. The rest wouldn't come. There was nothing after two. She'd never let there be.

Marlowe's mouth worked. "Cup," he said.

"...What?"

"On the floor. By the couch leg." He didn't lift his head off the armrest. "I can get it if I go flat, and I can't go flat without this"—he meant the shoulder—"telling me about my life choices. So it's been down there since Teodoro went out to the board." A breath. "You've got two arms. I can see them from here."

Wren stared at him. She had rehearsed this in the dark of the tool void a hundred times. The accusation, the flinch, *something*. She had not rehearsed a water cup.

"You don't know who I am," she said.

"Should I?" His eyes closed. "You're the lid-hand. Slate says Bay 4. That's more name than I had two days ago, so congratulations, we're even."

"I counted you down."

"Did it work?"

"What?"

"Am I down?" One eye opened, wet and irritated. "Because I'm sitting up, and I'd like a drink, and I'd like it before the bell. So whatever you think you did, you did it bad."

Wren crouched and got the cup, a dented steel thing, half full, and put it in his working hand. He drank like it was the point of the whole business. To him, maybe it was.

From the doorway Coombs cleared his throat. He had the tender's remote in one fist and the proving slate under his arm, and he wore the patient look of a man paid by the settled thing.

"That's the remand," he said, nodding at her wrists like the tape was still on them. "You've all been reading it wrong." He came a step in, genial as a stove. "A hold order doesn't execute at a node. Can't. A node's a closed roster. You lift a body off a closed roster, now you've got two rosters out of balance and a desk that notices. It only executes where a coast line can take you off my hands clean." He let it sit. "One place on this line does that. The switch stand at the Weir. That's where your count gets settled, lid-hand. Not here. Here you're just a woman who wants to be heard." He tipped the slate toward the door, the dark, the ore line, the cold coming up off it. "Tender rolls at the bell. Whatever you're gonna say to him, say it on the way. After the switch it stops being yours to say."

Wren looked at Marlowe. Marlowe had his eyes shut again and the empty cup against his chest, gone somewhere a shoulder didn't hurt.

The bell was twenty-eight minutes out.

Outside, the cold took the warm room off Wren's face in one pull. Anza's ore stub was four lamps and a lot of dark, and the dead med rig sat under a tarp at the end of it with a clean square hole in its dash where the transponder used to be — the box that tells a board where a rig is, so the board can pretend to care.

"Wrists," Rhea said.

Wren put them out. Rhea pulled the roll of seal tape from her coat, gray and stiff with cold, printed every hand's width with a receiving mark: BAY 4 SHIFT 2, the code a bay stamps so anyone downstream can see whose hands took delivery. Three turns, pressed flat with her thumb, torn with her teeth.

"You're quick at that," Wren said.

"Forty times a shift. Tape is the only thing out here that doesn't change its story." Rhea cut the tail short and put it in her pocket instead of the bin. "You, on the other hand, cut a seal in a tool void with a seam knife."

"You'd have done it too, if you'd been the one holding the lid."

"I'd have said one," Rhea said. "There's three numbers. You stopped at two like the last one costs money."

"It does."

Teodoro had the board ledge open on his knees, keying with two fingers, breath going up around his face. "Slate carries you as Bay Four lid-hand," he said. "Hands with a bay number where a badge goes. That's a live entry, so nobody shoots you on sight, and it's good exactly as far as the switch, because past the switch a coast roster line takes a body off the slate and writes whatever it likes in the name field. I can't hold it longer. I tried the hold-order field and the field tried me back."

"Comforting," Wren said.

"You want comforting, go be cargo." He sealed the ledge. "Also your man in there refuses to countersign himself off the plate. I've asked twice. He said he's shop crew and shop crew doesn't quit before the bell."

Nour came out of the shop with the last spare cartridge in one fist — the little brass-throated canister that scrubs a respirator's air until the diaphragm quits — and the draw-line key in the other, the sprung brass handle that opens Anza's resupply draw and keeps the node's chain green.

"I'm not standing out here watching a tender leave," she said, and pushed the cartridge into Rhea's coat. "That's Ivo's. It goes in at minute forty or he starts sounding like a bad pump. I've got the draw. Nobody at this node eats until I say, and I say at shift change."

"Twenty-six minutes," Rhea said. "If the switch goes wrong—"

"Then be wrong somewhere with a knife and a name," Nour said, and went back in, and the shop door dropped and sealed behind her.

Miko was already up on the shelf over the motor box, boots braced against the coolant loop, arms wrapped round her knees, looking like a woman who had found the good seat on purpose.

"The Weir's the coast switch," she said, when she caught Wren looking. "Two years I've been buying my way to a green board. I'm not sitting out a night in a relay shop because somebody's got two numbers left to say."

"You're not coming back."

"Not to anything with a roster on it, no."

Coombs swung up onto the deck plate with the remote in his fist and thumbed it twice. The tender cranked over — a low shudder up through the deck, the sound of a machine that did not need any of them — and the slate on his hip woke and read the stub: four bodies, one of them a bay number.

"Board says clear to the switch," he said. "Ninety kilometers. Coast lights off the trestle if the air's dry."

Wren stepped up. The tape on her wrists caught the lamp, BAY 4 SHIFT 2, three turns, tight.

Then the slate gave one soft note on Coombs's hip, by itself, with nobody within four meters of it but the dark up the ore line.

Miko sat up. "What was that?"

Coombs looked north for a while. "Nothing on the stub," he said.

"Nothing on the stub," Coombs said again, mostly to the slate, and put the tender out onto the ore line.

The four lamps went behind them and the tarp and the dead rig with the square hole in its dash, and then there was dark on both sides and cold coming up off the ballast. The deck plate took the cold first. The shelf over the motor box didn't, and Miko had found that out inside a minute, sitting on the coolant loop — waste heat off the motor, piped through the shelf on purpose — with her boots braced and her arms round her knees like a woman at a stove.

"Warmest seat on the Interior," she said. "Whoever built this rig liked runners."

"Runners," Coombs said from the deck plate, genial as a lit oven. "That's the coast word for a body that walked off a shift contract with wet boots. I haul you back, the roster feeds you, the bunk's hot, and nobody asks what you did in a tool void." He let that sit. "Offer's open at the switch, lid-hand. Open the whole way down."

"Sell it to somebody who's cold," Rhea said.

"One rule aboard, and it's her rule, not mine." Coombs tapped the dash, where a bar of light in the nose read the top of the rail ahead and told the motor what it had found. "She reads the rail. Reads clear, she starts. Reads blocked, she stops. She don't read weather and she don't read you. You could stand on the shoulder waving both arms with your name in lamps and she'd hold forty right past you."

"A body on the rail?" Miko said.

"Then she stops. Then she starts again in ninety seconds, and you'd want to be off it before that."

Miko already had Rhea's seam knife out, the short thin one for opening cargo wrap without breaking the seal, and was working under the dash lip at a palm-sized plate, four bolts and a gasket.

"Transponder," Rhea said. "Answers a board's hail with a number and a position. Cut it, the rig's nothing to any board on the line."

"Never keyed." Miko tipped the plate into her coat and patted the pocket. "Factory blank. No number, no bay, no owner. That's how he runs a tender that posts nowhere." She lay back on the warm pipe. "There's a woman at Culvert Nine trades flour for a plate with no number on it. Can't trace a blank back to the bay that stamped it."

"She'll trade. She won't hand anything over, and she'll weigh it in front of you."

"Everything's weighed."

Rhea went hunting the brakes, because that was the hole the rule left. If the rig stopped for nothing that wasn't rail, the thing that stopped it was under her hands and she wanted its name. Air first: two reservoirs slung under the deck, a line running forward to the shoes at every wheel, the compressor ticking off the motor. Air shoved the shoes onto the wheels. Lose the air, lose the brakes.

Then, in a bracket behind the motor box, a folding steel arm with a socket on the end, and below it a wedge on a screw, greased, the paint worn off the top where hands had been.

"Reseal," Wren said. She'd come up the deck without Rhea hearing her, tape bright on her wrists. "Bay 4 spur had one. For when the air let go."

"Talk me through it."

"You crank. Screw drives the wedge down till it bites the rail, and friction does the rest." Wren looked at it a moment longer than she needed to. "Forty-two turns."

"Forty-two."

"Then you find out if it's enough."

The crank came out of the bracket heavier than it looked, and the handle was worn bright, the way a tool goes bright when it's used a lot by people in a hurry.

"How many times has this rig needed it?"

Coombs didn't answer that. He was watching the line.

Rhea put her palm flat on the coolant loop to warm it. Hot enough to take skin, nine minutes into a run the board called flat.

"Is she working?"

"She's pulling."

"On the flat?"

"Ore line's all grade," Coombs said. "Some of it's just polite."

Rhea put the crank back in the bracket, within reach of the deck, and left it there. Ahead the gauge sat steady in the green and the rails went into the dark reading clear.

Coombs told them it was thirty there, and then he proved it by standing at the dash with his thumb over the remote, the little dead-man box that could tell the motor to stop. One press was a slow-down. Hold it three seconds, the placard under his thumb said, and you got the whole thing.

Past the board the ore line dropped into a cut, its walls still furred white on the north side where yesterday's sun hadn't reached, and the tender went into it at forty and did not come out.

"Hold it," Rhea said.

"I'm holding it."

"Then hold it harder."

"It's all the same hold." Coombs's thumb had gone white. Three seconds, four. The gauge sat in the green. NOMINAL, it said, which was the air system's way of saying it had enough of everything. Air was the argument, and air was fine. Pressure shoves the shoes on. Lose the air, you lose the brakes. She'd read that board a hundred times and never once caught it lying.

Miko sat up on the shelf. "He's got a brake that works on no air. Why's he not using that?"

"Because a wedge on the rail at forty is how you meet the rail," Wren said. She was at the bracket, and the crank was already in her hands. "Reseal's iced."

She knocked the crank's socket heel against the screw housing. The ice came off in a gray plate and rang on the deck.

"It isn't the air," she said. "It's the shoes. The wheels are wearing ice, and you can't push a shoe onto ice. Your board can't see grab. All it sees is pressure." She set the crank in the socket. "Forty-two turns. Somebody get on the pin."

Miko came off the shelf and sat on the deck with her boots against the cleat and her shoulder into the wedge pin, the fat steel peg that kept the screw from walking. Rhea tore a strip off her gasket-tape coil with her teeth and wound the screw housing three times, flat and tight, so the ice couldn't get back in while it turned.

"One," Wren said, and leaned.

"Is she working?" Coombs said.

"Two."

"She's reading rail. That's all she does."

"Three. Four."

The cut walls went by close enough to touch. Rhea kept her eyes on the gauge and the gauge kept saying NOMINAL, and she believed it, because she always had, and because the alternative was believing the woman with the tape on her wrists.

"Nine. Ten. Eleven."

"Miko, is it moving?"

"It's moving." Miko's heels were skidding on the deck plate. "Slow."

"Fifteen. Sixteen."

"Wren." Coombs had both hands on the tarp rail. "If that wedge hangs up down here, she won't see it. She'll hold forty till the Weir and the Weir's a curve."

"Twenty." Wren's breath came in white rags. "Twenty-one."

The needle never moved. Rhea watched it the way you watch a man who's lying to your face, and it kept right on lying in the same calm green.

"Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine."

"Say something useful," Miko said through her teeth.

"Thirty-one." A grunt. "Thirty-two."

At thirty-eight something went out of the sound under the deck, the high skating note quitting all at once, and the deck jumped, and Wren kept counting.

"Thirty-nine. Forty. Forty-one."

The wedge bit. The tender sat back on itself so hard that Miko went flat on her back and Rhea caught the crank bracket and hung there while the wheels locked and skidded and the ice came off them in sheets and the whole rig slewed sideways down the cut and stopped with its nose a body-length short of the bend.

Nobody said anything for a while. The motor ticked.

"Forty-two," Wren said.

Coombs let the rail go, finger by finger, and looked at his slate, and swore once, without heat. "Eleven minutes. The Weir lines up for the coast at the top of the hour and not one minute past. That's my margin gone, lid-hand."

"Then don't stop for anything that isn't rail," Wren said.

She counted back to zero, and Coombs thumbed the remote, and the tender picked itself up and went on like the last four minutes had happened to somebody else. The gauge said NOMINAL. Behind them the cut stood empty.

Rhea put her hand flat on the coolant loop and left it there. Eleven years she'd believed the glass over any mouth on the line. She listened to the wheels instead, which was not a thing she had ever done, and did not like how easy it was.

"Coombs. Is the plate in there steel or composite?"

His eyes went to the dash, and stayed there a second too long.

“Composite,” Coombs said. “The plate’s composite. It doesn’t ring.”

“Then what sang at the stub?” Wren asked.

“Ask the road.”

Rhea looked back down the ore line. “A steel plate sings. A composite plate doesn’t. You’re telling me the slate heard something that isn’t there.”

“I’m telling you the slate heard two names it had no business hearing, and one of them is standing on my deck.” Coombs keyed the handset clipped to the dash—a yard set, short-range, good for a relay and not much else. “Anza, tender.”

Static. Then two headlights came up the ore line behind them.

No running lights. No marker lamps. Just the two white eyes and, under them, a shape with the same empty square in its nose where a transponder plate should have been.

Miko sat forward. “That’s an empty mount.”

“I pulled the only blank,” Coombs said.

“You pulled one blank,” Rhea said.

Coombs thumbed the handset. “Rig behind, this is the tender ahead. You are on a live line. Answer.” The headlights held their distance. “Rig behind.”

“Try the board,” Miko said.

“She don’t post,” Coombs said. “That’s why she’s behind us.”

The handset crackled. “Coombs.” Kass’s voice, thin and fast, with the relay shop’s compressor whine under it. “Don’t stop.”

“Kass, I have a rig on my tail with no lights and no plate.”

“I know. I’ve been pulling vanished rigs off the old ghost roster. The fleet’s real, and it’s bigger than five. They don’t post because they can’t. Blank mounts, all of them.” A pause, keys clacking. “Kettering’s morning desk answered the remand. Released it early. That’s all it answered.”

Coombs looked at Wren. “The switch is live.”

“It was always live,” Kass said. “Now it’s early. And File 2244 is rolling. Physical recovery. A crew and a body box, out of Kettering for Anza. They’ll be at the node before the next bell.”

Rhea’s hand went to her coat, to the cartridge for Ivo, then stopped. “Marlowe can’t be moved.”

“Tell him that. I did. He said he’s shop crew and shop crew doesn’t quit before the bell.”

“Kass—”

“I’m not dropping it,” Kass said. “I’m just telling you what’s coming while it’s still coming.”

The headlights behind them did not gain. They did not fall back. They held forty, exactly forty, the way a machine holds a thing it has read and decided.

“She’s reading our rail,” Wren said.

“She’s reading her own,” Coombs said. “Same line. Same grade.”

The tender went down into the cut, and the gauge sat in the green. Then the grade fell away, hard, the deck tilting forward under their boots.

Miko said, “Coombs.”

Ahead, the trestle came out of the dark with ice sheeting both rails.

The trestle was four hundred meters of steel deck laid across the spillway, a concrete channel wide as a yard, built to carry flood water off the high country and dry since before any of them drew a shift. Under the deck the dark went down to a floor of white stones.

The tender went on at thirty and quit in the middle of it.

"Full stop," Coombs said. He had the remote in both fists now, thumb down, the placard under it worn shiny. "Three seconds, that's the whole thing she's got, and it's doing nothing, because there's nothing for it to do it with. No grab." The gauge said NOMINAL, calm as a preacher.

"She reads the top of the rail," Rhea said. "Ice is smooth and it shines. To that bar of light in the nose, that's clean rail."

"Then it's clean rail and I'm the liar." His thumb stayed down.

The deck came level. Then it tipped the other way, and the tender went backward up the grade, slow, and getting less slow.

"Backward," Miko said. "We're sliding backward. There's a rig behind us coming forward. Somebody do that arithmetic out loud for me."

Rhea had the tape off Wren's wrists before anybody answered. Three turns, cut with the seam knife, BAY 4 SHIFT 2 going over the side into the dark.

"I didn't ask," Wren said.

"You were about to. You do a thing with your hands first."

Coombs already had the crank out of the bracket, socket seated. "Give it here, lid-hand. Slate's on my hip and it writes down what a body does. Every turn you put in goes on you as Bay 4 hands, and that's more rope than you want at a switch. Let me carry them. Your proof stays what it is."

"My proof." Wren took the crank out of his grip, which took some doing, because he didn't hand it over so much as lose it. "My proof is two numbers and a man who won't let me finish them. You can't clean it by doing my job for me."

"I can try."

"Hold the light, then."

Miko was already down on the deck plate, boots against the cleat, shoulder into the wedge pin — the fat steel peg that keeps the screw from walking while it turns. "Same as the cut," she said. "I'm the cheapest thing aboard and I'm not stepping off at a switch that isn't there yet."

Rhea wound the screw housing with gasket tape, three turns, flat, biting the end with her teeth. Coombs went to the dash and keyed the yard handset. "Anza, tender. We're stopped on the Weir trestle with the brakes iced and a rig on the line behind us." Static, and the compressor whine somewhere under it, and nothing else. He keyed it again. "Anza."

Wren set her weight on the handle. "One."

The drop was under the deck, four hundred meters of steel between the wheels and white stone, and the deck was moving, a hand's width every few seconds, patient about it.

"Two. Three. Four."

"Coombs, the handset—"

"She don't answer when she's got her hands in a board," Coombs said. "Keep counting, lid-hand."

"Nine. Ten." Wren's breath came in rags. "Eleven."

At fourteen the handle took her. Bare steel at that temperature welds to skin, and she pulled the turn through anyway, and Rhea heard the sound of it, small and wet, under the count.

"Fifteen. Sixteen."

"That's your hand," Rhea said.

"It's a hand." Wren didn't look at it. "Seventeen. Eighteen."

Rhea had cut a disc out of a glove palm ten hours ago, clean, with a knife, in a warm room, to keep her brother's chest moving. That had been a neat piece of work. This was not neat, and it was the same hand.

"Twenty-two. Twenty-three." Blood was going round the handle in the turns now, marking them. "Say something useful or shut up."

"The wedge is moving," Miko said, through her teeth. "It's moving, it's moving—"

"Twenty-nine. Thirty."

The deck slid a foot and stopped sliding, and started again, slower.

"Thirty-five. Thirty-six. Thirty-seven."

"Coombs," Rhea said, "if it doesn't bite—"

"It bites or we find out what's at the bottom of a dry spillway," Coombs said. "Forty is the number, lid-hand."

"Thirty-eight. Thirty-nine. Forty." A grunt that came up from her boots. "Forty-one."

The wedge went down the last of the screw and found the rail, and the whole tender sat back on itself so hard the crank rang, and the sliding quit. The pin held. The deck stopped moving. Below it the channel went on being dry.

"Forty-two," Wren said, and let go, and stood there with her hand open at her side, not looking at it.

Coombs keyed the remote. The motor picked up, found grab it didn't have, and spun.

At the far end of the trestle, behind them, two white eyes came up onto the deck and stopped. The slate on Coombs's hip gave one soft note, with nothing within four meters of it.

PASSAGE_END
